channel.description: Recent content in External Memory on Algorithmica

item.title: Memory Hierarchy
item.description: No single storage technology simultaneously provides tiny latency, enormous capacity, persistence, low energy use, and low cost. Computer systems combine several technologies and keep active data near the processor while colder data remains farther away. The words higher and lower are ambiguous here. Some authors call L1 “high” because it is at the top of a diagram; others call a storage tier “high” when it has greater capacity. This chapter avoids both terms.

item.title: Virtual Memory
item.description: Programs manipulate virtual addresses. The operating system and processor translate those addresses to physical memory or to another backing object, while enforcing permissions for each process. This indirection provides isolation, sparse address spaces, shared memory, file mappings, and demand paging. Virtual memory does not mean that every allocated byte already occupies DRAM. Reserving an address range, committing storage for it, making its pages resident, and writing it durably to a file are different events.

item.title: External Memory Model
item.description: The RAM model charges the same unit cost for every memory access. That is often the wrong abstraction when data movement crosses a cache, storage, or network boundary in blocks. The external memory model, also called the I/O model, keeps one such boundary and discards most other detail. Aggarwal and Vitter used it to derive tight bounds for sorting and related problems in their foundational I/O-complexity paper. #The ParametersMeasure all three quantities in the same unit, usually fixed-size records:

item.title: External Sorting
item.description: If $N$ records fit in memory, sorting is an ordinary in-memory problem. When $N>M$, repeatedly comparing records through random file accesses is the wrong interface. External merge sort turns the work into long sequential transfers and uses memory to merge many streams at once. In the external memory model, optimal comparison sorting takes $$ \operatorname{Sort}(N) =\Theta\left( \frac{N}{B}\log_{M/B}\frac{N}{B} \right) $$ I/Os, where the logarithm is at least one. Multiway merge sort attains this bound.

item.title: List Ranking
item.description: A linked list is easy to traverse and difficult to lay out. If successor nodes occupy unrelated blocks, following $N$ pointers can cause $\Theta(N)$ I/Os even though the records themselves occupy only $\Theta(N/B)$ blocks. List ranking converts that pointer structure into numeric positions without assuming that list order matches storage order. #Define the Rank FirstLet every record contain a unique identifier, a successor identifier or null, and a nonnegative edge weight $w(v)$.

item.title: Eviction Policies
item.description: A cache with room for $k$ blocks eventually sees a request for block $k+1$. If all resident blocks are still eligible for reuse, one must leave. An eviction policy chooses which one. The classic paging model assumes equal-size pages, equal miss cost, and a known sequence of page references. Real caches may store variable-size objects, charge extra to write dirty data, prefetch, or serve requests concurrently. The simple model is still useful, but its conclusions should not be silently transferred to a different cost model.

item.title: Cache-Oblivious Algorithms
item.description: A cache-aware algorithm chooses tiles, buffers, or fan-in using known $M$ and $B$. A cache-oblivious algorithm contains no parameters tuned to those values, yet its access order can still have an asymptotically good block-transfer count. The usual analysis uses an ideal fully associative cache with $M$ words, blocks of $B$ consecutive words, and optimal replacement. Results often assume a tall cache, $M=\Omega(B^2)$. These are proof assumptions, not a description of every CPU.

item.title: Spatial and Temporal Locality
item.description: The external memory model counts transfers using precise $M$ and $B$. Early in an optimization, those parameters may be unknown or the real machine may have several relevant levels. Two qualitative ideas remain useful: Spatial locality: after accessing one address, the program soon accesses nearby addresses that may share a transferred block. Temporal locality: after accessing a value, the program reuses it before the cache evicts it. Neither is a guarantee.

item.title: B-Trees
item.description: A balanced binary search tree needs $\Theta(\log_2 N)$ nodes on a root-to-leaf path. That is excellent when nodes are already in cache. If every node is on a different storage page, however, a lookup performs one random I/O per comparison while using only a few bytes of every page it fetches. A B-tree changes the unit of progress. One node occupies one block and contains many sorted separator keys, so a single I/O chooses among many children.

item.title: Sublinear Algorithms
item.description: To compute the exact sum of an arbitrary array, we must inspect every element: an unread value could change the answer. The same obstacle applies to an exact maximum, an exact number of distinct keys, or a complete list of frequent items. If even one block may contain decisive information, no clever layout makes an exact algorithm sublinear. Approximation changes the question. Instead of “return the answer,” we ask for an estimator whose error is at most $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$, or for a deterministic summary with a stated additive error.

item.title: Memory Management
item.description: new looks like a primitive operation, but it crosses several layers. C++ establishes an object’s lifetime, a user-space allocator finds suitably aligned storage, and the operating system eventually maps virtual pages to physical memory. Most calls stop at the allocator’s fast path; some refill a shared pool; a much smaller number request pages from the kernel. This separation explains two common surprises. Allocation can be expensive without making a system call, because it may contend on shared metadata or miss in caches.
